chapters.name: Chapter 1: Making your device easier to see and hear

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Making text bigger and easier to read
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make the text on your phone or tablet larger and bolder.
This lesson builds toward: Using the Settings app on your phone or tablet, you will make the text larger and bolder and zoom in on a screen, until text is comfortable to read.
Small text is one of the most common reasons people give up on a phone. The good news: every smartphone and tablet lets you make text larger, and many let you make it bold too.
Menu names differ from phone to phone, so the easiest way is to search. Open the Settings app (often a gray gear), tap the search bar at the top, and type "text size" or "font size". Tap the result and slide the bar to the right until the text is comfortable. Look for a "bold text" switch nearby as well.
Some apps also let you zoom in by placing two fingers on the screen and spreading them apart. Pinch them together to zoom back out.
Step by step:
- Open the Settings app.
- Tap the search bar at the top.
- Type "text size" or "font size".
- Slide the bar to the right until text is comfortable.
- Turn on "bold text" if you like.
Words to know:
- Settings: the app where you change how your phone looks and works, usually a gear picture.
- Font: the style and size of letters on the screen.
- Zoom: making what is on the screen look bigger.
Try it now: Open Settings, search for "text size", and make your text one or two steps larger. Open your messages or email to see the difference.
You can now make the text on your device larger and bolder.

check.q: What does spreading two fingers apart on the screen do in many apps?
check.why: Spreading two fingers apart zooms in; pinching them together zooms back out.

check.q: You cannot find the text size menu on your new phone. What do you do?
options: Open Settings, tap the search bar and type "text size"
Turn the phone off and on
check.why: Menu names differ, so searching Settings is the easiest way to find the setting.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Your phone as a magnifier and reader
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use your phone to magnify small print and to read text aloud.
This lesson builds toward: Given small print such as a medicine label, you will use the phone as a magnifier and turn on read-aloud, so you can read or hear the print.
Your phone's camera can work as a magnifying glass for medicine labels, menus and receipts. iPhones have an app called Magnifier. On many Android phones you can use the Camera app's zoom, or search Settings for "magnif".
Phones can also read text aloud. Search Settings for "spoken content" or "select to speak", and turn it on. Then you can select text and choose Speak. Google Lens and some AI assistants can also read a photographed page aloud.
Turn on the flashlight if the light is dim, and hold the phone steady a few inches above the page.
Step by step:
- Open Magnifier, or the Camera app and zoom in.
- Hold the phone a few inches above the small print.
- Turn on the light if needed.
- To hear text, search Settings for "spoken content" or "select to speak" and turn it on.
- Select text and choose Speak.
Words to know:
- Magnifier: a tool that makes small things look bigger on your screen.
- Read aloud: when the phone speaks written words out loud.
Try it now: Use your phone to magnify the small print on a food or medicine label. Then turn on the read-aloud setting and have your phone read one message to you.
You can now magnify small print and have your phone read text aloud.

check.q: What is the Magnifier app on an iPhone for?
options: Using the camera as a magnifying glass
check.why: Magnifier turns the camera into a magnifying glass for small print.

check.q: You want your phone to read a long article aloud. What do you search for in Settings?
check.why: Turning on spoken content or select to speak lets you select text and choose Speak.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Captions and hearing help
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn on captions so you can read what is being said.
This lesson builds toward: When voices on videos or calls are hard to hear, you will turn on captions and find your phone's hearing options, so the words show on screen.
If voices on videos or calls are hard to hear, captions show the words on screen as they are spoken.
Many phones have a feature that adds captions to almost any video or audio, called Live Captions. Search Settings for "caption" to find it and turn it on. In YouTube, tap the CC button on a video. Many video call apps also have a captions button.
Phones can also connect to many modern hearing aids by Bluetooth. Search Settings for "hearing" to see what your phone offers, and ask your hearing care professional which settings fit your hearing aids.
Step by step:
- Open Settings and search "caption".
- Turn on Live Captions or captions.
- On YouTube, tap CC on the video.
- On video calls, look for a captions button.
- Search Settings for "hearing" for hearing aid options.
Words to know:
- Captions: words shown on the screen as people speak.
- Bluetooth: a wireless way to connect your phone to things like hearing aids or speakers.
Try it now: Search your Settings for "caption" and turn captions on, or open any YouTube video and tap CC. Watch one minute with captions.
You can now turn on captions on your device and find hearing settings.

options: Adds captions to almost any video or audio on the phone
check.why: Live Captions shows the words of videos and audio on screen.

check.q: You want to connect your hearing aids to your phone. What is a good first step?
options: Search Settings for "hearing" and ask your hearing care professional
check.why: Settings shows hearing options, and your hearing care professional knows which fit your aids.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Setting medicine and wellness reminders
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set a daily repeating reminder for a medicine or healthy habit.
This lesson builds toward: Given a medicine or healthy habit, you will set a daily repeating reminder on your phone, at the time your doctor or pharmacist said, checked that it is set.
A daily reminder on your phone can help you take medicines on time, drink water, or take a short walk.
The easiest way is to ask your phone's voice assistant: "Remind me to take my morning pill every day at 8 am." You can also open the Clock or Reminders app, add an alarm or reminder, and choose that it repeats every day.
A reminder only helps you remember; it does not tell you what to take. Always follow the instructions from your doctor and pharmacist, and ask your pharmacist if you are unsure about timing. Some pharmacies also offer free refill reminders by text or app.
Step by step:
- Ask your voice assistant, or open the Clock or Reminders app.
- Say or type what to remember and the time.
- Choose that it repeats every day.
- Check that it is set.
- Follow your doctor's and pharmacist's instructions.
Words to know:
- Repeating reminder: a reminder that comes back every day or week without setting it again.
- Refill: getting more of a medicine you already take.
Try it now: Set one daily repeating reminder for a medicine you already take, or for a healthy habit such as a 10-minute walk.
You can now set a daily repeating reminder for a medicine or healthy habit.

check.q: What does a repeating reminder do?
options: Tells you which medicine to take
Comes back every day at the time you chose
check.why: A repeating reminder returns daily; it helps you remember but does not tell you what to take.

check.q: You are not sure whether to take a pill before or after breakfast. Who do you ask?
check.why: Follow your doctor's and pharmacist's instructions, and ask your pharmacist about timing.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Preparing for a doctor's visit with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use an AI assistant to turn your concerns into a clear list of questions for your doctor.
This lesson builds toward: Before a doctor's visit, you will use an AI assistant to turn your concerns into a short list of clear questions, with no private numbers and no medicine changes because of AI.
Doctor's visits can feel rushed, and it is easy to forget what you meant to ask. An AI assistant can help you organize your thoughts before you go.
Describe your concerns in general words, without your name, birth date or insurance numbers: "I have a checkup next week. I have been more tired than usual, my knees ache on stairs, and I want to ask about my blood pressure medicine. Help me make a short list of clear questions to ask my doctor."
AI is for preparing, not for diagnosing. Do not change or stop any medicine because of what an AI says. Bring your list to the visit, write the doctor's answers down, or bring a family member to help.
Step by step:
- Write your concerns in general words, with no private numbers.
- Ask AI for a short list of clear questions.
- Put the most important question first.
- Bring the list, and write down the answers.
- Never change medicine because of AI; ask your doctor.
Words to know:
- Diagnose: to decide what illness or problem someone has; only a medical professional can do this.
Try it now: Think of your next appointment. Ask an AI assistant to turn two or three of your concerns into a short list of questions. Check that it has no private numbers, then save or print it.
You can now prepare a clear list of questions for your doctor with AI, safely.

check.q: What is AI useful for before a doctor's visit?
options: Organizing your concerns into clear questions
check.why: AI is for preparing your questions, not for diagnosing.

check.q: You are writing your concerns for the AI. What do you leave out?
options: Your name, birth date and insurance numbers
That you have a checkup next week
check.why: Describe concerns in general words, without private numbers.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Finding trusted health information
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check health information on a trusted, free source.
This lesson builds toward: Given health information from AI or a website, you will check it on a trusted source such as MedlinePlus, your doctor or your pharmacist, before you act on it.
Health information online ranges from excellent to dangerous. AI assistants can also be wrong about health. So check what you read with a trusted source.
MedlinePlus (medlineplus.gov) is a free health information site from the National Library of Medicine, part of the US National Institutes of Health. It has no advertising and explains conditions, tests and medicines in plain language. Your doctor's office and your pharmacist are also trusted sources.
Be wary of sites that sell a cure, promise miracle results, or tell you to stop your medicine. When something you read worries you, write it down and ask your doctor or pharmacist.
Step by step:
- Notice health claims from AI or websites.
- Look them up on medlineplus.gov.
- Ask your doctor or pharmacist about anything that worries you.
- Avoid sites that sell cures or promise miracles.
Words to know:
- Trusted source: a reliable place for information, such as a government health site or your own doctor.
- MedlinePlus: a free, ad-free health information website from the US National Library of Medicine.
Official sources:
- About MedlinePlus (National Library of Medicine)
Try it now: Final task: change one setting to make your phone easier to see or hear, set a daily reminder for a medicine or a walk, and use AI to make a short, private-number-free list of questions for your next doctor's visit. Look up one topic from your list on medlineplus.gov.
You can now make your device easier to use, keep up with daily health habits, prepare for appointments, and find trusted health information.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Easier to see or hear No setting changed. Changed one setting for seeing or hearing, such as bigger text or captions. Changed two or more settings and can show someone else how. Daily reminder No reminder, or it does not repeat. A daily repeating reminder for a medicine or walk, checked that it is set. The time matches what the doctor or pharmacist said. Clear questions No list, or the questions are vague. A short, clear list of questions made with AI help, most important first. Has space to write down the doctor's answers. Private numbers kept out The prompt or list has a name, birth date or insurance number. No private numbers in the prompt or the list. Concerns are described in general words that still give the doctor a clear picture. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: A free, ad-free health information site from the National Library of Medicine
check.why: MedlinePlus explains conditions, tests and medicines in plain language, with no ads.

check.q: A website says a tea will cure your blood pressure and you can stop your medicine. What do you do?
options: Treat it as a red flag, write it down and ask your doctor
Stop your medicine and try the tea
check.why: Sites that promise cures or say to stop medicine are red flags; ask your doctor or pharmacist.
